title: HoYoverse's Nodusfall is free to play but isn't a typical gacha game: 'Characters are not obtained through random draws'
text:
If you watched the Nodusfall trailer during Gamescom's Opening Night Live and, like me, thought the combo of Elden Ring's aesthetic and Monster Hunter's fights sounded awesome, but were worried about selling your soul to the god of gacha, fret not!
Nodusfall isn't just a visual departure for HoYoverse, swapping the vibrant anime aesthetic for something gloomier, it also represents a (partial) change in business model.
According to the devs, "Nodusfall will be a free-to-play, long-term game. What we can share at this time is that characters are not obtained through random draws. We hope to allow players to unlock this core gameplay experience through continued play. Cosmetic monetization is an important avenue we will be considering."
In my hands-on, the four available characters could be customised with different outfits, hairstyles and accessories, and I can imagine folk dropping some cash on some new fits for their boss-slaying crew, but it's a relief to know that I won't need to go through RNG hell or wipe out my bank account just to play as a surly warrior who can transform into a dual-wielding giant.
Gamescom is absolutely full of the typical anime cast gacha games this year, so it's a pleasant surprise to see the studio best known for them trying something a wee bit different. It feels different, too. Not like Genshin or Zenless Zone Zero, but not exactly like Elden Ring or Monster Hunter, despite them both being obvious inspirations. The fights are a bit more forgiving, for one, and also snappier and more fast-paced.
I've only just finished sending a trio of bosses back to whatever afterlife they go to, so I've still gotta digest what I played, but Nodusfall definitely makes a great first impression. Check back in the next couple of days for my full hands-on preview.

title: New GTA 6 character swapping details revealed: Jason and Lucia can 'play as a couple, or go off and cause chaos independently'
text:
We've got more Grand Theft Auto 6 details to chew on, and this time not from a vegetable . An interview in magazine Dazed has revealed a bunch of details about the design of GTA 6, including how character swapping between protagonists Jason and Lucia works.
We'll get straight into it. Here are the most notable details from the interview:
1. Exercise and diet
Dazed says that food will affect Jason and Lucia's weight, and "exercising visibly builds and tones their muscles." Playing for long periods without sleeping will also impact their appearance.
Rockstar has played around with these life sims systems in past games—most recently in Red Dead Redemption 2, where Arthur could gain or lose weight based on his diet. GTA hasn't had systems this granular since 2004's GTA: San Andreas, in which CJ could gain weight and lose it through working out.
2. Character swapping
The way GTA 6 handles multiple playable characters will differ from GTA 5. The Dazed preview notes that you can "choose to either play as a couple, or go off and cause chaos independently." They described a scenario where you can cruise along the highway as Jason, then swap to Lucia in the passenger seat to "scroll on the in-game phone."
That sounds, to me, like GTA 6 will have a dynamic 'couple mode' for open world roaming—in keeping with this being a love story—but missions themselves might be solo or together.
3. Rockstar's team size
According to Dazed, Rockstar has massively expanded its team and resources to get all the details in GTA 6 right. The studio has more than doubled in size since Red Dead Redemption 2. It has an office in LA dedicated to the pedestrian NPCs that fill the open world. It also brought in over 50 real world street artists to help design the murals for GTA 6's version of Wynwood, Miami's outdoor art galleries, and there's a team of actual race car drivers handling the vehicle physics.
4. Expect to see a variety of Florida Men
Per Dazed: "Players can expect encounters with virtual iterations of Florida Man, the cultural archetype-turned-meme known IRL for wrangling alligators, drunken antics, and literal grand theft auto."
5. On music
Regarding GTA 6's music, senior vice president of narrative Ruper Humphries told Dazed:
"We love Miami music, particularly Miami bass, going through to more recent Miami artists like Kodak Black and Sexyy Red. We were also really interested in how the hip-hop scene in Miami exists in house parties in Overtown, clubs like Booby Trap on the River, and then high-end places on South Beach where bottles can cost thousands of dollars. We needed characters who could take us through those worlds."
6. Jason and Lucia's backgrounds
The preview notes that Jason is ex-military and a drug runner. Lucia is an amateur fighter (as seen in trailers) fresh out of prison.
7. Choices
Dazed suggests that player choices or behavior will affect Jason and Lucia's relationship in ways that "cut much deeper than Rockstar’s previous titles or 'honour' systems."

title: I got my greasy mitts on a host of RTX Spark laptops running, what else, games at Gamescom 2026—and there's a couple I really want to take home
text:
Hello from Gamescom 2026 , where yours truly has been trying out some of the latest laptops at the Nvidia booth. The machines I was shown are made by various manufacturers, but all of them have the same core internal hardware, in the form of Nvidia's RTX Spark SOC.
Which means that, alongside 20 Grace CPU cores in the custom Arm-based chip, they've also got 6144 RTX Blackwell GPU cores to play with. And that means RTX 5070 -like gaming performance, at least on paper.
And in practice, each was demonstrated to be capable of running modern games at high frame rates. Exactly how high was kept under wraps, unfortunately, although it was mentioned that frame generation was in use for each.
So, I wasn't able to do any benchmarking of my own, or dig into the settings menus to find out exactly what sort of DLSS/FG combination I was dealing with. Still, 007 First Light , Arc Raiders , Borderlands 4 , and F1 25 were all running without a hitch, which is apparently indicative of the smooth sailing Nvidia has experienced with Microsoft's Prism translation layer .
I asked about any unforeseen emulation issues, but nope, apparently all is well in the land of Windows-on-Arm and Nvidia chips. As for the laptops themselves, I took a few notes based on my brief time playing with them at the booth.
Future Future First off, lets talk about the one I really want to take home. The Asus ProArt P14 looks and feels, for all intents and purposes, like the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 —and that's a very good thing indeed. It's got a milled aluminium chassis that feels robust (yet slim in the hand), a crisp keyboard, and a beautifully vivid OLED panel.
I had a brief run around in Arc Raiders on this particular lappy, and immediately wanted to squirrel it back to my hotel room for a proper gaming session.
14-inch laptops are the perfect size for taking on the road, and the relative lack of weight compared to the beefier (and much older) Blade 15 Advanced in my backpack made me yearn for the little P14 instead.
Proper gaming performance, too? It appears so, although Arc Raiders is far from the most demanding of test games. Still, while I'm not so confident in my abilities as to guess exactly what frame rate or settings combo this machine was running at, I will say it felt like 100 fps+. Ah, go on then. Probably High to Ultra settings. If I was pushed. Maybe.
Special mention should also be given to the Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition . Yes, I associate Dell laptops with being dull as well, but this new XPS model feels excellent, and it's rather handsome, too. The keyboard is as tight as a drum, the OLED display looks great, and it wasn't making a whole lot of noise while I ripped and teared my way through Doom: The Dark Ages .
(Image credit: Future) It feels like a civilised machine I'd be happy to sling in my bag, at least on this first impression. Both of these laptops look like the sort of thing you might expect to see in a business meeting, but the gaming ability of the RTX Spark SOC squeezed into their slim and light chassis designs is plain to see.
Every laptop showdown, even one as brief as this, is likely to come up with an also-ran that doesn't quite cut the mustard—and for me, this comes in the form of the new Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra . In a room full of sublime competition, the chassis looks and feels... tired, while the Mini LED screen wasn't particularly enticing to behold. It was trundling away in the corner of the room running World of Tanks , and didn't garner "oohs" and "ahhs" in the same way as the rest.
(Image credit: Future) Despite the hardware inside, something about it says "old fashioned" to me. It's funny how we judge these things in an instant, but there we are. I'm prepared to change my mind if we get one in for review (I'm incredibly tired and cranky after a long day at the show, after all), but I get the feeling it's going to cost lots of money—without looking and feeling as good as its premium competition.
Ah, now I've gone and done it. I've mentioned the price. Or rather, prices. The Nvidia reps around me refused to be drawn in on exact figures for these Spark-infused machines, especially as some of the models on display had a loadout of 128 GB of RAM. Ludicrous amounts, I think you'll agree, which will almost certainly be sold for ludicrous amounts of cash. For all that local AI stuff you'll be doing, naturally.
Personally, the lesser-seen optimist living in the middle of my cold, brutal heart is still hoping for 16 GB or 32 GB variants of the Asus and Dell laptops for somewhat-reasonable figures—as more slim and light, gaming-capable machines to choose from is always a good thing.
Looking at the state of gaming laptop prices at the moment, though, I think said optimist will probably be let down once more. It was a nice day out, at least. Anyone fancy buying me a bratwurst?

title: Game of Thrones: War for Westeros isn't even out yet and it already feels ancient
text:
"But why?" That's the question I kept asking myself as I played through a few skirmishes of Game of Thrones: War for Westeros , an RTS based on HBO's TV show. It's a competent, workmanlike creation that nonetheless fails to capture any of what made the show and the books that inspired it such a phenomenon.
It just feels so ill-timed, too. It's not due out until 2027, but Game of Thrones concluded in 2019, with a final season that even GoT defenders such as myself had to acknowledge was a bit of a dud. These days, HBO is busy with its prequels: the plodding but still entertaining House of the Dragon, and the delightful, brisk A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms.
(Image credit: Playside) Instead of giving us something new, or even current, War for Westeros returns us to the fight for the Iron Throne. You can command a tiny Kit Harrington, listen to narration from Charles Dance, or enjoy a rendition of The Rains of Castamere while you build another mine. These touchpoints are too recent to engender feelings of nostalgia, but not recent enough that they elicit much excitement.
Now, don't get me wrong. GoT provided us with some of the greatest battles to ever grace our TVs. Even as the story went off the rails, the muddy brawls were a sight to behold. There's plenty for an RTS to take advantage of—but this style of RTS fails to play to the strengths of the source material.
GoT's gargantuan pitched battles call to mind the epic scale of Total War—it's no surprise that there are several GoT Total War mods. War for Westeros, meanwhile, has been fashioned in the mould of Age of Empires, or its fantasy cousin, The Battle for Middle-earth 2.
(Image credit: Playside) You plonk down buildings that generate resources, which you can spend at other buildings that spit out troops or let you research upgrades, and then you send your army to capture territory or boldly torch your opponent's HQ. You can build fortifications and siege engines, but most of your conflicts will be between generic soldiers, sometimes led by heroes drawn from the show's roster of important folk.
It's fine, I guess. There are certainly worse GoT games—most of them on mobile. But War for Westeros is so straightforward and plain that I probably would have had more fun with something uniquely awful. A bawdy brothel management game with Littlefinger, perhaps?
Where Age of Empires had a multitude of bespoke civilisations to play around with, and The Battle for Middle-earth 2 was full of exotic fare like giants and goblins and horrible spiders, War for Westeros is simply full of dudes. Squads of spearmen, squads of swordsmen, slightly smaller squads of elite Night's Watch warriors.
(Image credit: Playside) The full game will feature four factions, but I was only given access to arguably the dullest: the Starks and Lannisters. No dragon-loving Targaryens or hordes of the undead for me. Of the two, the Starks are the most conventional, though they can field direwolves, as well as troops drawn from the Night's Watch and the Free Folk. The Lannisters, meanwhile, are more economy-focused, featuring quirks like a debt mechanic that allows you to quickly fund expansion.
So there's some asymmetry, but that's par for the course. And at least where the Starks and Lannisters are concerned, the asymmetry is broad rather than exciting. It's hard to get pumped about one faction needing to spend a wee bit more gold to recruit their slightly better swordsmen.
OK, maybe I'm being unfair. There are more substantial differences than that. Like being able to recruit both Stark heroes' fluffy pets, which bumps the available heroes up to four (with a fifth locked in the preview build). That's double the Lannisters' roster. There are some more unique units, faction-specific upgrades and special mechanics—but they all fell a bit flat for me. It's all just very, very dry.
(Image credit: Playside) The nature of this type of RTS means that it's never going to give you memorable fights like the Battle of the Bastards or titanic Total War-style clashes, but after a few upgrades you can field some pretty meaty armies and get some big, messy scrums going. The rather plain aesthetic does mean that they aren't always the easiest to read, however, or particularly engaging to watch. That said, I am a fan of the physicality of the cavalry charges, which send any infantry units that get in the way flying.
The big problem is the lack of an obvious hook. This is an extremely conventional RTS, and while the genre isn't especially healthy at the moment, there are still plenty of alternatives. If you're in the market for something fairly traditional, Age of Empires 4, Age of Mythology: Retold or Tempest Rising have a lot more going for them.
The GoT skin is simply not enough to carry it, and there was little that felt uniquely GoT about the skirmishes I played. Perhaps the campaign will inject some much-needed flavour into the proceedings? The more exotic Targaryen and Night King factions might spice things up a bit, too. But so far, it's just very safe and predictable.

title: GTA 6 leaker escalates spoilers, releases 4 minutes of Lucia's prologue
text:
The most anticipated game of all time continues to spring leaks. The mysterious Cyberleek , an individual who apparently has access to a build of GTA 6 and has been attempting to profit from it with a meme coin ever since, has released the biggest chunk of the game yet.
This time, it's not just joyrides and beating up random civilians: The 4 minute 38 second clip is all early Lucia story content. This is the first time Lucia, GTA 6's co-lead, has made an appearance in Cyberleek clips, which until today have focused on the other protagonist, Jason.
A message superimposed in the video reads:
"This build is actually recent and the game is not ready at all. Sony and Rockstar are killing your right to own and resell your games and Rockstar is killing their own employees too, the work required to reach gold is way too much for so little time left. Trading volume/price is how CL measures your support. CL will not continue without support. You decide."
It is certainly the most spoilery these leaks have gotten so far, and the escalation seems intentional. Cyberleek seems unsatisfied with the money they're making from the leak spree, and is doubling down on their supposedly altruistic motive while pushing their crypto. Or perhaps Cyberleek can feel the heat of Rockstar's lawyers fast approaching and hopes to squeeze more cash out of the adventure before the book is thrown in their direction.
While you should obviously avoid watching this one if you don't want to know anything about the GTA 6 story going in, I have a feeling Rockstar will reveal a lot more than this about its two main characters during the big Netflix reveal happening tomorrow.
More details about GTA 6's world and mechanics came today in the form of an early preview from youth magazine Dazed, which touched on how food and exercise will affect Jason and Lucia, how character switching works, and Rockstar's dedicated research team embedded in Miami.

title: Poppy Playtime studio reveals its next survival horror game, and this time it's co-op
text:
As a former employee of Playtime Co., you've explored the depths of its horrifying toy factory and met many of its inhabitants, including Huggy Wuggy, who just wants to hug you (to death).
Today Mob Entertainment, makers of Poppy Playtime , have announced a new game, and it's sending you back to that haunted toy factory once more—but this time you can bring some friends along. Escape from Playtime is a co-op horror game for 1-4 players and it's coming to early access on Steam. Here's the announcement trailer:
This time around you're playing "from the perspective of the cute-yet-disturbing Smiling Critters," says Mob Entertainment—the Critters being the misfit toys you meet in the original episodic (and singleplayer) Poppy Playtime.
"Tasked with scavenging materials for a mysterious building project that promises escape from the factory, players will need to work together and follow instructions from an ominous voice lurking somewhere in the shadows, all while evading the factory's most dangerous denizens," the developer says.
"Along the way, players can solve puzzles, uncover clues, scavenge tools, use hiding spots and alternate routes, and turn the factory layout to their advantage. Proximity voice chat adds another risk: communication is essential, but an irresponsible whisper can bring the mission to a brutal end."
Fans of the original horror series will see some familiar sights in the factory, but just because you've been there before doesn't mean there won't be a few surprises: "The mysterious Voice seems to be altering the factory's layout, creating procedurally generated environments that change with each run," says Mob Entertainment.
Well, a spooky factory full of mechanical horrors sounds like a great fit for co-op, so I'm not surprised Mob decided to make their next survival horror game a multiplayer experience. There's no date shown in the trailer, just that Escape from Playtime is "coming soon" to early access. Here's its home on Steam while you wait.

title: Blue Dragon has been stuck on the Xbox 360 for 20 years, but no longer: a fantastic unofficial PC port unlocks the FPS, goes 4K, and even adds mod support
text:
When Final Fantasy creator Hironobu Sakaguchi left Square Enix in the early 2000s, he started a new studio, Mistwalker, to keep making RPGs. For the last 20 years, every single one of his games with the exception of Fantasian has been stuck on one defunct console or another, never ported or re-released. And that's a shame, because some of them are great RPGs.
(Image credit: Mistwalker) Or I should say it was a shame, until now—because as of Friday, Blue Dragon will be playable on PC thanks to a fan-made port that's likely far more impressive than an official release ever would've been.
re:Blue, a static recompilation of the Dragon Quest-inspired JRPG, follows in the footsteps of the unofficial Sonic Unleashed PC port that proved how effective fan-made ports can be. These projects cleverly translate the original game code to run natively on modern PCs, but don't include any of the original assets to avoid copyright issues.
This technique has proven so popular that it's inspired a wave of AI vibe-coded ports that don't take the time and care to thoroughly adapt the original game to PC. But in spite of that, the good projects—like the recent Zelda: Twilight Princess port —have made it one of the most exciting things happening in games right now .
"My standards have always been pretty high when it comes to this kind of stuff—I like to make quality products," says Tom, the programmer behind re:Blue as well as ReXGlue, a toolset meant to help developers create more recompilations of Xbox 360 games like Blue Dragon. Tom introduced ReXGlue earlier this year, but has spent much of 2026 working on his port of Blue Dragon as a showcase for what his tools are capable of.
Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Some other ports have beaten Tom to the punch by quickly releasing rough works in progress, but re:Blue is by far the most polished and fully featured recompilation built using ReXGlue. And the game deserves it: while it looks very much like Dragon Quest thanks to Akira Toriyama's art, there are some fun RPG class system ideas and turn order jostling hiding within what at first appears to be a rudimentary turn-based system. More importantly for Tom, he's got backup from several superfans helping develop the port, and it presented a juicy technical challenge: a three-DVD game built on an engine that has never been documented.
I've been playing early builds over the last month, and have been surprised by how much better it looks and runs on my PC than many Japanese PC games did in the 2000s.
Just take a glance at the feature list:
Resolutions up to 4K, windowed or fullscreen
Aspect ratios 16:9, 4:3, 16:10, 21:9, 32:9, plus auto and stretch
Four quality presets, Low through Ultra
MSAA up to 8x or SSAA up to 4x
Anisotropic filtering
Shadow quality and draw distance
Field of view adjustment, 45 through 120 degrees
Unlocked frame rate, with optional caps at 30, 60, 90, or 120
The field HUD can fade out once you stop pressing anything, or stay off entirely
Achievement list viewable in game, with eight new re:Blue achievements alongside the original ones
Fully native keyboard and mouse support with cursor and look modes supported by mouse
Custom input based icons/glyphs for HUD elements, following the device you last used or pinned to Xbox, PlayStation, Switch, or Steam Deck
It works on the Steam Deck. It has a mod manager. It seamlessly combines the game files from Blue Dragon's original 3 DVDs into one executable. Itt fixes up tons of funky graphical effects that didn't scale well from the Xbox 360's original 720p resolution.
re:Blue, Mistwalker re:Blue, Mistwalker re:Blue, Mistwalker re:Blue, Mistwalker re:Blue, Mistwalker And all the new features Tom built for re:Blue integrate into the original UI so seamlessly that you could mistake them for elements that were there when the game released in 2006.
Inside the recompilation
(Image credit: Mistwalker, re:Blue) "Going into this, I was fairly naive that a lot of this could be generalized," Tom says. "But [now] I don't know how much of that is true. When it comes down to making it look nice, and the features, that's all going to be game-specific. I think that's the beauty and the distinguishing factor between emulation and recomps. With emulation you're going to get the original thing, and it's probably going to play pretty damn well. Good enough for most people. But if there's a group of people crazy enough to want to port a game to PC, this is where they would come and find ReXGlue and spend the time to make it look good. Put the effort in, and not just make it a standalone emulator, really, which I think there's no value in. There is value in adding extra quality of life features."
Prior to re:Blue, ReXGlue ports have technically been using a hybrid of recompilation and emulation—to grossly simplify things, the CPU code was recompiled to run natively while the graphics were handled by an implementation of Xbox 360 emulator Xenia. Much of the work for Blue Dragon has gone into building a native renderer tailored to the game engine and modern PC graphics cards.
"When we talk about game-specific engines, we're thinking about: How does this build a scene, how does it simulate that scene, render that scene, and how is it presented? What are the subsystems? How do they talk? You start naive. To add the config menu, I started digging into the assets, seeing if I could get a window to pop up. Then I started digging into the functions to see how the game creates windows; that's a pretty involved process that can take days, months for some people.
"That's probably the hardest part about this: how you get the recompiled code in a way that you can inject extendable parts to make it a true PC port. The more you iterate, the more you're going to understand the engine, its quirks, how it works, and these small building blocks start to build a larger structure and the architecture starts to form. Then we're getting pretty close to a decomp , and that's when stuff starts getting really fun. That's happened in the last month or two: We've got a lot of these building blocks that are making something cool. How can we take that next step? And that next step became increasingly easier the more we had reverse-engineered and reimplemented."
For re:Blue, Tom and his collaborators had to tackle visual elements like bloom, gamma, and even overscan—because Blue Dragon was originally released in late 2006, it was still designed with CRT TVs in mind—to look correct on modern displays. They also had to work around its hard-coded 30 fps lock with frame interpolation to support smooth animations at higher framerates even as the logic still ticks along at 30 Hz.
Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue Mistwalker, re:Blue He credits Unleashed Recomp as a big inspiration for ReXGlue and a marvel of optimization that pushed him to make re:Blue run as efficiently as possible.
(Image credit: Mistwalker) " Skyth , the guy who worked on a lot of the rendering backend, is incredibly smart, an absolute wizard," he says. "They set the precedent on what performance and compatibility should be like, so we tried to strive for that. A lot of his stuff was the basis for how I optimized… to achieve the lowest [system specs] we could compatibility-wise."
If you have a GPU with at least a gig of VRAM, you should be set for re:Blue—and it'll run at a nice 1080p, 60 fps on the Steam Deck without taxing the handheld.
After months of iteration and testing, the 1.0 release of re:Blue is out Friday and will be available on GitHub , timed to the 19th anniversary of Blue Dragon's release in the US. But it won't mark the end of the project. While Tom will be porting some of the work he's done for re:Blue back into ReXGlue, his team also has plans for more updates and mods for Blue Dragon, including one that will insert the Nintendo DS sequel's characters into the original game.
They hope that mod will be just the start of a vibrant scene focused on Blue Dragon now that it's finally playable on PC.

title: Gamescom 2026 live hub: The latest news and previews from the biggest gaming event of the year
text:
Gamescom coverage sponsored by
(Image credit: Microsoft) This coverage brought to you by Fable, out February 23, 2027 for PC, Xbox Series X/S, and PlayStation 5.
Gamescom 2026 is underway. In this E3-less world, Gamescom is the biggest gaming convention of the year, and we've got multiple reporters on the scene in Cologne, Germany to check out as many games as they can.
I've also heard tell of a "horse controller" appointment. That's all the detail on that I currently have, and if you also want to know more, check back here for updates throughout the week.
Gamescom runs through August 30, and we'll be maintaining this hub even beyond that date as our writers continue to file stories, and we learn more about the games revealed and announced at the show.
Gamescom events
Opening Night Live recap
(Image credit: CD Project / Wizards of the Coast / Krafton) Gamescom kicked off with the Opening Night Live showcase hosted by Geoff Keighley. Here's our recap of all the big ONL trailers and announcements.
Future Games Show schedule
(Image credit: Future) Our friends at the Future Games Show are putting on three shows at Gamescom this year; see the full FGS Gamescom schedule here .
The GTA 6 reveal
(Image credit: Netflix, Rockstar) The GTA 6 reveal wasn't technically part of Gamescom, but it's the biggest thing happening this week. We've picked apart a bunch of details here.
Gamescom GDQ
Like seeing games, but done quick? The famed Games Done Quick speedrunning event has a Gamescom edition, streaming on Twitch and YouTube across three days, August 28-31.
Top Gamescom news
The Witcher 3 Remastered announced
(Image credit: CD Projekt) In September, Witcher 3 owners will get another huge free update called The Witcher 3 Remastered . It's not just graphics: the patch will touch combat, traversal, and more. We also saw the new Witcher 3 expansion that's coming next year.
Finally, a Lego city builder
(Image credit: Paradox Interactive) It just makes sense, doesn't it? Lego Skylines was revealed at Opening Night Live , and is described as a "cozy, customizable city-builder."
Paradox's next grand strategy game revealed
(Image credit: Paradox) Instead of history, Paradox is exploring post-history with its next strategy game , Afterworld, which is set in a post-apocalyptic North America.
More news
Warlock , the next big D&D game, got a lengthy gameplay trailer
Rainbow Six Tactics revealed: the first singleplayer R6 game in a long time
There's a new PUBG game and it's set in the '90s

Metro 2039 devs say the ongoing war in Ukraine has changed how they write morality: 'The franchise's very nature is getting too close to reality'

Live blog
August 26, 2026 – 3:56 PM The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past interview
PC Gamer's Josh Wolens is presently at Gamescom in Cologne, but before the convention, he travelled to Warsaw, Poland to talk to CD Projekt all about The Witcher 3's new expansion. Check out that interview above.
August 26, 2026 – 4:05 PM "Is it AI?"
Whether or not you care about the giant argument playing out over generative AI, the discourse is pretty inescapable during big videogame reveal events like Gamescom. Alongside "when's it out" and "can you pet the dog," the internet now also wants to know: Is it AI?
Sometimes, it is AI. But false positives happen, too. One trailer accused of being AI-generated on social media—and I admit that it also triggered my mental AI detector—was the live action announcement trailer for Humankind 2.
But the studio says that , actually, the trailer was filmed with "real actors, practical sets, and custom-made props."
August 26, 2026 – 5:28 PM A 'gacha' question
(Image credit: HoYoverse) The just-announced Nodusfall from Hoyoverse looks cool, but prospective players who aren't into the gacha scene the company is known for—games that are monetized primarily through loot box-like random rewards—may be put off by the assumption it'll be more of the same.
This game will be different, though, according to the developers, though the only specific commitment made is that characters won't be unlocked by random draws.
"Nodusfall will be a free-to-play, long-term game," the devs tell us . "What we can share at this time is that characters are not obtained through random draws. We hope to allow players to unlock this core gameplay experience through continued play. Cosmetic monetization is an important avenue we will be considering."
August 26, 2026 – 7:37 PM Metro 2039 looks great, but my GPU is sweating
(Image credit: Deep Silver) As Morgan pointed out , the new Metro game looks fantastic —fun, yes, but also in a literal, visual way—and those of us with aging PC hardware might finally be reaching the point where putting off an upgrade is no longer viable if we want to keep playing the latest and greatest at frame rates we're happy with.
I bought a new GPU right before the big crypto-driven GPU price hike, and then missed the brief window where the tech industry started behaving at least somewhat normally again before the AI boom once again drove up prices. The next time I hear a rational statement from someone in Silicon Valley, I'd better take the opportunity to pounce. Could be a long time, though.
August 27, 2026 – 7:16 AM Total War: Warhammer 40k reveals its campaign structure—also you can stuff Space Marine heroes in Dreadnoughts if they get banged up
As part of its special Gamescom livestream, Creative Assembly has dropped a tonne of new info about Total War: Warhammer 40k, including:
Each star system will make up a campaign, with about ten potential campaigns in a Crusade Theatre, letting you carry characters and armies between them.
Heroes will have 'followers' they can equip to change the unit composition of their bodyguard. Imagine something like the Imperial General's retinue in Dawn of War.
All unit weapon loadouts are fully customisable.
There are planetary governors who you'll have to appease to unlock certain diplomatic actions and support.
Space Marines can co-opt Planetary Defense Armies from the Imperial Guard to follow them as backup.
The Imperial Guard have a variety of structures they can build on planets (similar to forts or watchtowers in Medieval 2 and Rome Total War), including artillery batteries and deathstrike missile launchers.
My favorite new reveal is that 'almost dead' Space Marine heroes can now be turned into Dreadnoughts and keep fighting for The Emperor—a much-requested feature from the community.
August 27, 2026 – 9:44 AM Warlock's take on D&D magic might make me willing to sell my soul
(Image credit: Invoke Studios) Invoke gave us an even deeper look at its upcoming D&D game, Warlock—and it's looking stellar enough to have Fraser consider some pacts of his own . You can read his full impressions in the article I just linked, but just for your sake, here's a quote while he's off roaming the Koelnmesse. Don't say I never gave you nothin':
"After the methodical, measured chaos of Baldur's Gate 3, I find myself really in the mood for this more action-dense, almost DMC or Bayonetta-style approach to D&D magic. It's flashy and over the top, but there's still this tactical grounding. Invoke's got something pretty cool brewing here, and I'm keen to see more as it gets closer to its 2027 launch."

title: The Witcher 3 Remastered: Everything new coming in the big free upgrade
text:
After 11 years, The Witcher 3 is getting a new story expansion and a remaster. CD Projekt Red has announced The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered, which is coming in 2026 and will be a free upgrade for all current owners of the game, paving the way for the shiny new DLC coming next year. It isn't just a technical update, either: CDPR is making changes to The Witcher 3's combat, skill system, and hey, transmogs!
Witcher 3 Remastered release date
(Image credit: CD Projekt Red) The Witcher 3 Remastered release date
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered launches on September 29, 2026 . That's only a month away from the day it was announced, which is a treat! It was revealed just before the teaser trailer for the new expansion Songs of the Past, but that's not coming until 2027.
The remaster is a free update and the original DLCs are now free
The Witcher 3 Remastered will replace the current "Complete Edition" on storefronts when it launches in September. It will also be a free upgrade for anyone who already owns the base game The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. The original two story expansions Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine have also been made free for all base game owners in an update the same day as the remaster announcement.
There's a good chance you do already have those expansions either from the Game of the Year edition years back or the more recent Complete Edition that's been the default version for sale since 2022. If not though, they're yours now!
Witcher 3 Remastered features
(Image credit: CD Projekt Red) Here's what CDPR told PC Gamer about the remaster
Our own Josh Wolens got to see The Witcher 3 Remastered (and the Songs of the Past expansion ) played at Gamescom in August and talked with CDPR about the upgrades a bit.
CDPR's executive producer of external projects Jakub Kutrzuba told Josh that it wanted to think about what The Witcher 3 would play like if it were launching in 2026.
"We put a lot of our time into how the game actually plays," says Kutrzuba. "So, the animation system, the camera work, small quality of life improvements, accessibility changes, enemy behaviour in combat, maybe the pathfinding for the roads, etcetera—these are areas of the game which we know could cause some frustration here and there.
"We went through all of them and asked ourselves, 'What can we do about it, without rebuilding the game from scratch?' And we have changed a lot… the game just plays smoother, you know? There's no immersion-breakers anymore, I would say."

title: I've played Heroes of Might and Magic 3: Remake, and I still can't believe we're getting 2 HoMMs in the same year
text:
After lying fallow for over a decade, Heroes of Might and Magic is enjoying a bit of a renaissance. Earlier this year, Heroes of Might and Magic: Olden Era launched into early access and will hit 1.0 in 2027. And now it's going to be joined by an old friend with a new look. The series' golden child, Heroes of Might and Magic 3, is back. Again.
HoMM 3 Remake is actually the third version of the third game in the series, which was remastered back in 2015. At a glance, however, you could be forgiven for assuming that it's a brand new entry, as it boasts a new art style along with a few more tweaks. But this is still absolutely HoMM 3.
(Image credit: Ubisoft) I took it for a spin over a couple of hours ahead of its Gamescom reveal, playing the simple campaign prologue and the Arrogance scenario—a popular map first introduced in HoMM 3: The Shadow of Death. It's a compact, well-paced adventure that I remember being a good place to start when you wanted to delve into multiplayer (or if you just wanted a fun comp stomp).
This remains true in the remake. It's a four-player deal, and each starting position is close to a second town of the same faction, rapidly expanding your ability to recruit big unit stacks and making it easier to support multiple heroes early on. With entrances to the underworld close by, and nearby shipyards letting you cross the tiny ocean, it gives you the full HoMM 3 experience extremely quickly.
I confess, however, that I did embarrass myself a little bit. It's been a while since I've played HoMM 3, but I've been playing Olden Era in early access, so I expected to crush the AI. Unfortunately, I spent too much time just mucking around and fiddling with my army composition, so by the end I'd been outpaced by my computer opponents. I'm still convinced I could have clawed my way back, but we'll never know.
(Image credit: Ubisoft) So this is largely the game you'll remember, but with some convenient quality-of-life improvements. Of particular note is the ability to see movement ranges for enemy troops, letting you identify which of your units might be at risk on the enemy turn—something that exists in the later HoMMs, but not HoMM 3 or its 2015 HD remaster.
If you don't remember because you never played the original, here's the skinny: you command heroes and their armies as they scoot off on grand adventures, hassling monsters, conquering towns and gobbling up resources. Inside those conquered towns, you can construct a plethora of buildings—most of which can be upgraded—allowing you to recruit more units and heroes, as well as unlocking new spells.
Each day lets your heroes travel a specific distance, and as time moves inexorably forward, your recruitment pool and treasury will expand, allowing you to field larger armies and more heroes. You'll eventually have hordes of dragons, giants, angels and demons ready to smite your foes in grid-based battles.
(Image credit: Ubisoft) The hallmark of the series—and 3 in particular—is how easy it is to get to grips with, which belies its impressive depth. There's an accessible lightness to the proceedings, accentuated by a frequently whimsical tone, that eases you into a level of complexity that would otherwise be daunting. There are so many layers to juggle—economic management, big-picture strategy, tactical combat, RPG systems, and then the literal layers, as you try to conquer both the overground and underground regions.
HoMM 3 was exceptional in 1999, and age has not tarnished it.
The most obvious change in the remake is the art style, and this is something I'm a bit more ambivalent about. It's vividly colourful, fantastical fare, with units that are considerably more detailed than its predecessor's. The combat animations are cracking, too, making each attack more dramatic and weighty. The quality is there, then, but I fear the soul might be lacking.
(Image credit: Ubisoft) OG HoMM 3 simply had a bit more character, with big, bold monster designs. It veered towards the cartoonish, certainly, but these goofy-looking units had a lot of rizz. The remake may have smoothed out the edges too much, aiming for fidelity over personality. And this is more obvious because we have another modern HoMM with which we can compare it.
HoMM: Olden Era's mere existence makes this remake pretty unusual. Olden Era is a completely new entry in the series, but it's obviously a spiritual successor to HoMM 3, both mechanically and aesthetically. It feels like a natural evolution. So it does feel bizarre to see it now sharing the limelight with a remake. There's just a heck of a lot of overlap.
Still, after waiting over a decade for more HoMM, I'm not going to turn my nose up at two coming along at the same time. HoMM 3 Remake launches next year, and Olden Era should be leaving early access then, so tactics nerds will have plenty to keep them occupied.

title: Tim Curry, Red Alert 3 star and camp icon of stage and screen, dies aged 80
text:
Tim Curry, the beloved English actor beloved for his pantheon of iconic, award-winning performances on stage, film, TV, and videogame screen, has died at the age of 80. First reported by TMZ , Curry died late Tuesday night at his home in Los Angeles.
Curry first carved his mark in the public consciousness as the cross-dressing pansexual mad scientist Dr. Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, the 1975 film adaptation of which still maintains a cult following as a midnight movie phenomenon. From there, he secured a decades-long list of cherished roles—as Darkness in Legend and Wadsworth in Clue; in The Hunt for Red October, Home Alone 2, and Spamalot; as Pennywise in It and acting as a piratical foil to Kermit the Frog in Muppet Treasure Island.
Powerfully flamboyant, artfully unhinged, and charmingly insidious, Curry extended his talents to live action and vocal performances in videogames as well. He played the titular role in Sierra's first and third Gabriel Knight point-and-click adventures, and later voiced characters in Brütal Legend and Dragon Age: Origins.
But he reached the pinnacle of his powers as Premier Anatoly Cherdenko in Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3, where he delivered what may very well be the single most triumphant line read in the history of acting . Nobody had ever before conveyed such a captivatingly absurd cocktail of energies while saying the word "space," and it's likely that no one ever will again.
In a "Making of Gabriel Knight" feature included on the CD in 1993 , Curry said it was "very exciting" to contribute his presence to videogames, because he welcomed "any new way to infiltrate myself into your minds." And we certainly welcomed it, too.
Curry's public presence receded as his health declined in recent years. He underwent brain surgery after suffering a major stroke in 2012, which left him partially paralyzed and affected his short term memory. But he was nonetheless welcomed by an adoring crowd at a 50th anniversary screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show in October 2025—the same month he released Vagabond, his memoir chronicling his life and career.
In one of his last interviews, Curry told CBS News in 2025 that—while he wasn't "galloping towards" death—he wasn't afraid of it.
"I try to avoid it, as I think we all do," Curry said. "But I suspect that in the end, I will welcome it."

title: Brütal Legend is available free in honor of Tim Curry
text:
Tim Curry has died at the age of 80 , leaving behind a rich legacy in movies, television, and videogames. As well as playing Gabriel Knight, Premier Anatoly Cherdenko in Red Alert 3, and Arl Howe in Dragon Age: Origins, Curry voiced the villainous Doviculus in Double Fine's heavy metal epic Brütal Legend. To pay tribute to his passing, Brütal Legend is currently available for free on itch for a very metal 666 minutes. You can download it now, or claim it to download later.
Doviculus, Emperor of the Tainted Coil, is the extremely Cenobite-coded bad guy of Brütal Legend, who was originally going to be voiced by heavy metal singer Ronnie James Dio. "Tim Curry just has the perfect voice," Double Fine's Tim Schafer told USA Today of the casting decision. "When we told him this guy was not just big and tough, but also has this kinky side who, when hit with an ax, might scream in pain or squeal with delight, Tim laughed and said, 'Perfect for me.'"
This isn't the first time Double Fine has given their game away for free. Last time it was in honor of Ozzy Osbourne , who has a cameo as the Guardian of Metal shopkeeper in Brütal Legend, and likewise it was made available for 666 minutes. At the time of writing, that means you have a little over nine hours to claim it.

title: Total War: Warhammer 40k will let you stuff your 'almost dead' Space Marine characters into Dreadnoughts so they can keep fighting
text:
The Total War: Warhammer 40k Gamescom demo is underway, with lots of players getting their hands on the upcoming grimdark strategy game for the first time. Total War's content creators have been giving their impressions, but Creative Assembly also snuck in a new Alpha Strike livestream, and this is one of the biggest information drops we've gotten yet.
The stream finally reveals the campaign structure for Total War: Warhammer 40k, explaining that each solar system we fight through will comprise a campaign, as we battle across multiple regions on each planet. Once a campaign is done, we'll zoom out to the wider Crusade Theatre, where we can start a new campaign in another system, carrying through our characters and retinues. Apparently, there are about ten systems per theatre, culminating in a final battle on Armageddon.
It's not necessary to complete every campaign in a theatre, but it's already reportedly bigger than anything Creative Assembly has made before, including Immortal Empires. There were lots of other little information tidbits, too, including:
Heroes will have 'followers' they can equip to change the unit composition of their bodyguard. Imagine something like the Imperial General's retinue in Dawn of War.
All unit weapon loadouts are fully customisable.
There are planetary governors who you'll have to appease to unlock certain diplomatic actions and support.
Space Marines can co-opt Planetary Defense Armies from the Imperial Guard to follow them as backup.
The Imperial Guard have a variety of structures they can build on planets (similar to forts or watchtowers in Medieval 2 and Rome Total War), including artillery batteries and deathstrike missile launchers.
One of the best and most loreful additions, though, is that you can place 'dead' Space Marine characters inside Dreadnoughts (1:20:41 in the stream).
"It wouldn't be Space Marines if you couldn't take the mushed-up, almost corpse of a Space Marine, stuff it in a big metal tin can, and send it back into battle as a Dreadnought," says Will, Campaign Designer on Total War: Warhammer 40k. "There will be a little mechanic where even if your character has died, they might continue to serve the Emperor in a slightly chonkier form.
"Dreadnoughts and Land Raiders as well, we're treating them more like characters. Like these are super rare, super powerful ancient creations that are really valuable."
(Image credit: Games Workshop, Alex Boyd) For those unfamiliar with Dreadnoughts, they're effectively what happens if you attach an array of deadly weapons to a life support sarcophagus and give it legs. Most mortally wounded Space Marines who are interred in them gradually lose their minds as they turn to mush over the long centuries, repeatedly roused from slumber to face each new battle, or provide wisdom and ancient memories to the younger brothers of the chapter.
Still, knowing that one of my Space Marine heroes who I've battled with since my first campaign can stave off permadeath by hopping into a Dreadnought is a great feature. After all, it sounds like we're going to grow very invested in our small, yet elite, self-created Space Marine retinue as we fight across the many campaigns of the Crusade Theatre.

title: Crimson Desert will be slowing down its free updates in preparation for its paid DLC, and I'm just glad Pearl Abyss is finally pacing itself
text:
You've got to give Crimson Desert kudos—it's been getting hit with free update after free update, including, most recently, an overhaul to the game's story . But that'll be slowing down in coming months, as Pearl Abyss gears up to release the game's first major paid piece of DLC content.
"While there still will be updates," says director of marketing and PR Will Powers in an interview with IGN at Gamescom 2026 , "I don't think the scope and scale and pace of them will be as consistent past this point. What we're taking this opportunity to do is shift our development resources from these regular updates to focus on the upcoming DLC."
And you know what? Good. Crimson Desert was already a systems-heavy game at launch with an absurd amount of stuff to do—but just look at what's been added already. 20(!) small critters, a shotgun , a ton of different chest types, difficulty options , new animal mounts and inventory management , the ability to have your own hoard of pets , boss rematches and legendary creatures. Birdwatching? Why not, put it on there .
This game is an everything bagel that has only had more everything bagel seasoning heaped on top. It is a glorious leaning tower of mechanics that somehow hasn't collapsed under its own weight. It is a monument to game development hubris and as much as I respect Pearl Abyss' energy and commitment, I think it's probably for the best that it slows down.
Not too slow, though. As Powers confirms, the paid DLC will still be aiming for a release sometime in the final quarter of this year, which is wild to me. I wouldn't have even blinked if Pearl Abyss decided it was coming later, but no—the Kliff train stops for no-one.
By the time the studio finally puts Crimson Desert down, it's going to be a mammoth of a videogame. This thing takes around 250 hours to complete , baseline. I suspect that by 2036, Crimson Desert will have created infinite energy, cured every illness in existence, and given Kliff a railgun or something.

title: Nvidia says it would be making a whole lot more money if it weren't for the memory crisis it's contributing to
text:
Nvidia's latest earnings call is in and, as you can probably guess, the GPU maker turned AI hardware creator is raking in cash hand over fist. But alas, a projected 70% revenue increase for the 2028 fiscal year is apparently conservative, as the blasted memory crisis is getting in the way. You know, that memory crisis, which Nvidia's AI aspirations are currently making worse.
When asked about that 70% figure specifically, CEO Jensen Huang confirmed that it's a "constrained" number that is informed by the lack of available memory in the market
Huang says, "The unconstrained would be a lot higher. We grew 100% year-over-year this year. The unconstrained is significant. And so we're just going to have to work hard to get more capacity. And we have a large supply chain".
Nvidia's financials paint an interesting picture, specifically one where data centers account for the majority of revenue, and consumer demand lacks in response. Nvidia made $96.2 billion in the latest quarter, with a gross margin of 75% and data center revenue accounting for $89 billion. That's a 117% jump from last year.
Annoyingly, Nvidia doesn't report gaming in financial earnings, and instead wraps it into 'Edge Computing', which includes gaming, workstations, physical AI PCs and robotics. That accounts for $7.1 billion in the latest earnings call. That's a 27% jump from last year.
(Image credit: Future) In regard to Edge Computing, Nvidia says "increases were driven by strong sales of Blackwell workstations, partially offset by slower consumer PC sales that were tempered by elevated memory and systems prices."
As of today, the RX 9070 XT and 9060 XT are sitting atop the Amazon and Mindfactory GPU sales . It's not yet clear if pricing, stock, or a combination of both are responsible for this shift.
Huang says many investors expressed concerns regarding gross margins with rising component costs, and confirms "we are experiencing extreme pricing conditions in memory. The magnitude of the price increase has exceeded our prior expectations and [is] headed even higher into next year."
However, he argues, "We have a really gigantic supply chain. And so we have incredible partners, and we've secured a lot of supply, but we just need a lot more."
It seems the memory crisis is really hitting everyone and is unlikely to end any time soon. Even the likes of Samsung has warned of a 'severe' memory supply crisis next year. Pour one out for poor old Nvidia, who will have to pay more for the fire it is currently throwing even more wood onto.

title: Konami is aiming for a new Silent Hill game every year with producer Motoi Okamoto trying to quell fears by promising fans that they 'will be able to provide positive kinds of surprises'
text:
Too much of a good thing, believe it or not, can be bad, even when that thing is Silent Hill. Especially when faced with the prospect of a new game every year, though franchise producer Motoi Okamoto has tried to reassure us that it's totally a good thing.
"Our aim is to, hopefully, have an annual release of new games," Okamoto says in an interview with GamesRadar at Gamescom 2026 . "We would like to let players know that we have more experiences coming up, and many types of games that, we believe, will be able to provide positive kinds of surprises for players waiting for this for the series."
(Image credit: Konami ) Silent Hill f was perhaps the most pleasant gaming surprise I've had in a long time. My expectations weren't exactly low for the game, but I was still apprehensive to see whether Konami and NeoBards could pull off a Silent Hill game which left behind the foggy American mountain town and did something different. But as you can probably tell from my glowing Silent Hill f review , they managed to pull it off.
They did such a great job, in fact, that it single-handedly made me excited for future games to take the curse of Silent Hill to new locations. So why am I so apprehensive about the idea of a new Silent Hill every year? Well, because I also used to play Call of Duty.
(Image credit: Screen Burn Interactive) What scares me most about an annual release is the pressure both development studios and devs at Konami may face to keep up. Silent Hill isn't exactly an easy formula to replicate, yes its atmosphere and vibes are distinctive, but it takes more than a bit of fog to pull it off. The key is having a story which is traumatic, believable, and substantial enough to not only justify the fog descending on the protagonist, but to also keep players interested.
Okamoto does at least understand the need for keeping the series fresh with new ideas, however. "If we stay laser-focused on the same American setting, that would exhaust [narrative] possibilities, and also potentially cause fatigue for the playerbase," he adds.
While teams need to "work within the types of environments and the types of storytelling that works best for them" they also need to push the boat out, creating new circumstances which justify new games. I never want to finish a new Silent Hill game and think to myself: 'I should've just replayed Silent Hill 2 '. Hopefully, it never comes to that.

title: I barely remember the last time Nvidia mentioned gaming at all in an earnings call
text:
When I hear 'Nvidia,' I still think 'gaming'. But after scrubbing through the company's latest earnings call , I'm not sure Nvidia's investor relations team is thinking much about gaming these days at all. In fact I had to go back through the records an entire year to find a time when it made one mention of it in an earnings call. That's how little impact it seemingly has on the company's bottom line.
That's not to say Nvidia isn't still doing gaming stuff. It's just released DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction to help clean up the artifacting in high-end ray and path-traced games, as well as showing off the upcoming RTX Spark laptops at Gamescom actually running games on their ARM-y insides.
But it couldn't escape our notice that none of Nvidia's board members so much as uttered the word 'gaming' to investors in last night's earnings call, once again . But with the data centre segment bringing in $89 billion this quarter alone, accounting for almost 93% of the company's total revenue, it's not hard to see where the company's priorities now lie, and why.
Nvidia made $96 billion in total revenue in the second quarter of 2026, doubling what it made during the same period last year. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress told investors, "The surge in AI demand is driving a global infrastructure buildout, supported by an expanding and diverse set of growth opportunities, spanning hyperscalers, AI labs, AI natives, enterprises and sovereign customers."
For those unclear, I'll explain the last part of this comment: hyperscalers handle massive AI workloads so need a lot of infrastructure like data centres. AI labs are at the tech's bleeding edge in terms of research and development. 'AI natives' refers to workflows, products, or companies that are built from the ground up around AI—in other words, it's an inextricable aspect from the start. Enterprise customers may have otherwise bolted on data-centre-dependent AI products at a later date. Finally, sovereign customers can represent either businesses or even entire countries that want to retain full control over an AI technology's entire lifecycle.
The really brain-melting thing though is that Kress adds that the company expects "to grow revenue by approximately 70% in fiscal 2028," even in the midst of the RAMpocalypse . In fact, Nvidia feels it would be making a whole lot more money if it weren't for the memory crisis it's contributing to . Still, even in a "supply-constrained" landscape, Nvidia is not expecting the demand for AI or data centres to slow down any time soon. That leaves gaming out in the cold.
(Image credit: Future) In fact, Nvidia no longer reports on gaming as its own separate segment. Instead, this has apparently been bundled up into the Edge Computing segment, which itself made $7.2 billion. Kress comments that these "increases were driven by strong sales of Blackwell workstations, partially offset by slower consumer PC sales that were tempered by elevated memory and systems prices." The Edge Computing segment saw a 27% year-over-year increase, though this win still pales in comparison to all things AI at Nvidia.
Obviously, Nvidia hasn't stopped selling its very shiny RTX 50-series GPUs—so shiny in fact, that it would have been genuinely cheaper for me to fly to QuakeCon and buy an RTX 5090 at the Nvidia booth than pick up the GPU absolutely anywhere else. But even though the RTX 5090 costs a small fortune, gaming is clearly not the priority it once was for Nvidia, nor has it been for a while.
The last time I remember Nvidia mentioning gaming in an earnings call was this time last year, and even then AI was already making 10 times as much as gaming . De-emphasising the gaming segment even further is something we could all have seen coming. With that in mind, hearing 'Nvidia' and still thinking 'gaming' before 'AI' or 'data centres' puts me firmly behind the times.

title: Linus Torvalds details his 'debug session from hell' pushing an AI to fix an error it repeatedly said was 'impossible and unsolvable'. He then made it write the report
text:
Linux creator Linus Torvalds has famously been fairly hot and cold on generative AI in coding work, seeing a good purpose for it whilst also acknowledging a lack of quality control has led to a flood of unhelpful reports . Well, it seems like AI won't be fully replacing him just yet, as he's recently undergone a 'debug session from hell' where his AI assistant recommended he give up several times.
As spotted by International Cyber Digest , Linus took to a Linux Kernel commit to state all it took was "fixing a bogus 'round_up()' to a 'round_down()', but there were 24 patches adding more and more debug information to this, and 18 kernel boot to finally narrow it down to this."
This is a good example of where an AI might struggle to fix code, because it's not a syntax error or a bug, necessarily. The function is technically 'correct', it's just not doing what Torvalds wants it to . "The AI several times stated flat out that this was impossible and unsolvable," says Torvalds, "and that we should just write a report about it."
It seems like grit, determination, and stubbornness were what got the AI to behave in the end. Torvalds says, "I suspect those things have been trained by people who may not be quite as stubborn as I am."
Torvalds does praise the AI he's using, noting that, "while the AI was ready to give up several times, it did keep adding debug code and analyzing it faithfully when I pushed. So credit where credit is due and I let the AI write the commit message above."
Linus Torvalds says tracking down a bug in Linux's Intel GFX Driver was a "debug session from hell." The AI helping him repeatedly called it "impossible and unsolvable" and suggested they just write a report instead.He kept pushing. 24 debug patches and 18 kernel boots later he… pic.twitter.com/lUcMnECd9S August 26, 2026
Generative AI in coding has proved to be somewhat contentious. Last year, Collins Dictionary awarded 'vibe coding' (coding with AI) the word of the year , and a paper at the beginning of 2026 argued that " vibe coding kills open source " due to the lack of human attention and the ability for anyone to contribute huge amounts of data.
AI vibe coding ports of old console games have even become a bit of an ethical battleground . The team behind DK64 Randomizer (as you might guess, it randomises Donkey Kong 64) has been developing an unofficial PC port, specifically saying "Fuck AI vibe coding bullshit."
That's because, ignoring environmental concerns of AI plus the ethically dubious sourcing of data for training , teams like DK64 Randomizer argue that reliance on vibe coding results "in a poor quality project that will make it progressively harder to manage as time goes on."
Some developers clearly argue the benefit of AI code right now, but even so, it seems a human touch is often needed.

title: The Witcher 3 Remastered makes the original's best HD mod obsolete, but only because that same modder's been working on the real deal
text:
It's been a long road, but a mod we called The Witcher 3's best graphics overhaul will no longer be needed—and for once, I can talk about a mod becoming obsolete with a smile on my face, because the reasons involved here are all good ones.
The Witcher 3 HD Reworked is a cornerstone of the game's modding scene. We're talking over 325,000 unique downloads (725,000 in total), and that's just the version that was uploaded back in 2024. The "OldGen" version , uploaded in 2015, has an eye-melting 1.7 million unique downloads (5.8 million in total). It's a frankly astonishing upscaling and remodelling project that effects thousands of textures, models, and so on in CD Projekt Red's classic.
It's so impressive, in fact, that CDPR just snapped the guy up for The Witcher 3 Remastered . HalkHogan writes : "It's been a while since the last news and I would like to clarify any questions and confirm that I am cooperating with CDPR on The Witcher 3 Remaster, and my work will be officially available in the game on September 29 (on PC and consoles). HDRP will no longer be needed.
"Almost all in-game characters, monsters, animals, vegetation, armors and equipment for Geralt & Roach and a large part of the environment have been reworked, and I've put a lot of effort into ensuring the highest quality. Thanks and see you later!"
This means that you're not gonna need The Witcher 3 HD Reworked anymore because, well, the guy who made it worked on the remaster. Our own Joshua Wolens spoke to executive producer Jakub Kutrzuba about it earlier this month: "We are integrating the most popular mod on Nexus mod, the HDD Rework mod, with tons of upgraded textures, meshes. [It's] something which is bringing great visual improvement across the whole game."
As for how it turned out, he took a peek more recently during Gamescom 2026, where he wrote: "It's something else now. Letten is gorgeous from all angles, whether you're watching the sunrise crest the hills or stepping into the oppressive darkness of its sinister woods."

title: Warlock's take on D&D magic might make me willing to sell my soul
text:
Warlock, Hasbro and Invoke's open world action romp , looks like a good time—at least if your idea of fun is using magic to steal an ogre's sword before tossing it at another horrible creature, or using fancy blood rituals to ruin a sunny day, bringing rain and gloom. "Creative use of magic," Invoke calls it. I call it being a magical party pooper, but I'm here for it.
OK, so here's the deal. You're Kaatri, an experienced swinger of swords who's made a deal with D&D celebrity Tasha—you might know her from such spells as Tasha's Hideous Laughter—who has gifted you with a wide range of tricks. I'm sure it's not going to be a deal that comes back to bite her on the ass. Weird goths offering power? Always trust them!
Since Kaatri had this whole other life before making a deal with Tasha, she doesn't exclusively rely on magic. She's perfectly capable of removing heads from bodies the mundane way, in melee scraps that look snappy and cinematic. How the melee actually feels, well, I'm going to have to wait to find out, as Invoke and Hasbro aren't handing over the controller just yet.
Honestly, though, I'm more interested in the magic—even if using a sword is sometimes a bit more efficient. Take a simple obstacle, like some nasty, stabby brambles blocking a path. Now, you could just chop them away with your sword, but you know what's cooler? Using the spell Tasha's Leash to grab a lamp, which can then be used to set fire to the brambles. If too much fire is the problem, then you can use the same spell to grab a bucket of water to put it out.
It strikes me that Kaatri might be a victim of Maslow's hammer. No, that's not another spell. It's the idea that when we become overly familiar with a tool, we start to see it as the solution to everything. If the only tool you have is a hammer, everything becomes a nail. Which is bad. But screw Maslow—magic is awesome, why wouldn't you want to use it to solve everything?
And to be fair to Kaatri, magic is a wide-ranging bag of tricks. In the demo, I get to see her Shadow-stepping all over the place, teleporting to and away from enemies, as well as through obstacles. Any heavy objects in her way can be deftly moved aside without her breaking a sweat, or even moving. And when she's faced with a big gap and an imposing drop, some magical tentacles build her a bridge. I wish hammers were this useful.
So magic is incredibly convenient for traversal and puzzles—and traversal puzzles —but seeing it used in combat is where it becomes downright seductive. This is why you make dodgy deals with witch queens.
I kinda hate when videogame combat gets compared to ballet—a deadly ballet, a lethal ballet, blah blah blah—but seeing Kaatri firing on all cylinders (all credit to the Invoke dev driving the demo) really is physical poetry. It looks elaborate, technical and elegant. Yes, I'm annoyed I didn't get to play myself. The stringing together of melee, teleporting, time manipulation and telekinesis is just a delight to watch. And the interplay between all these spells and attacks goes beyond the immediate, instantly gratifying stuff.
At one point, we see Kaatri summon a little table, at which she performs a blood ritual to change the weather. It starts to rain. Bummer. But this drizzle does more than make enemies sad and damp—it makes them more conductive. And Kaatri can hurl lightning at them. Now we're cooking.
After the methodical, measured chaos of Baldur's Gate 3 , I find myself really in the mood for this more action-dense, almost DMC or Bayonetta-style approach to D&D magic. It's flashy and over the top, but there's still this tactical grounding. Invoke's got something pretty cool brewing here, and I'm keen to see more as it gets closer to its 2027 launch.

title: 'It's just not our money to keep': Handheld console maker Panic is refunding US tariff fees to its customers
text:
Panic has been able to share some really good news this week to its customers. Those who bought the handheld console and were charged extra for its tariffs will be getting a refund.
"There was a specific window of time this year where we charged tariffs to customers," Panic co-founder Cabel Sasser explains in an email to Game Developer . "We tried absorbing the cost for a while, but that was financially difficult for a small company like ours. We made the tariff a very obvious and clearly labeled line item on checkout for any customer affected."
(Image credit: Panic Inc.) The US tariffs had a devastating impact on all sorts of physical games from hardware like the Playdate to tabletop and board games. Costs on all sorts of products which were manufactured outside the US increased significantly. But some respite has been had for the companies that've managed to secure a tariff refund from the US government, including PC cooling company Arctic , and now Playdate.
"It's just not our money to keep, and it felt really good to give it back," Sasser says. "That's an easy way to know you made the right decision." But as with anything the US touches, it's not exactly a painless process.
"Still, it took a lot of work for us to file all the paperwork to get the refund from the government," Sasser adds. "It took work to build a little system to process the refund, and sometimes it felt like, wait, why are we seemingly doing more work than even gigantic companies are on this issue? That felt weird. But I guess it makes sense in a way, because our small size means we’re far more directly affected by something like a tariff."
Oh, to be at the whims of an administration that acts first and thinks only when they're legally forced to do so. It's clear that Sasser would've rather spent time on literally anything else: "From start to finish on this whole tariff whim, all I could think about is all the cool stuff we could be working on instead." But at least customers are getting some money back after the whole fiasco.

title: What's the best starting class in Star Wars Zero Company?
text:
Picking the best starting class in Star Wars Zero Company is a little challenging when you haven't played any of the game yet. But don't worry: you can change your class specialization once you hit Cycle 3, which is very early on. After that point, you can also change the specialization and talents for hired operators too.
The only thing you can't tweak is named character talents, like Hawk's Fearless Leader. Below I'll offer my recommendation for the best starting specialization in Star Wars Zero Company, plus some options if you don't want to double-up classes with any of the named characters you initially team-up with.
Star Wars Zero Company best starting class
There are eight specializations to choose from (Image credit: Bit Reactor) The best starting class in Star Wars Zero Company is the Scoundrel . This specialization has a great kit focused around making enemies vulnerable (for guaranteed critical hits), penetrating their defenses, and increased assist damage. This ties in perfectly to Hawk's Fearless Leader talent, which increases assist damage for the whole squad when they're present. Assists are free attacks that also generate advantage, so they're very strong.
While you can respec any character specialization when you reach Cycle 3, the first three companions you'll get are a Scoundrel (Kabb), a Soldier (Trick), and an Assault (Jae). Having two Scoundrels in a party isn't a bad thing considering Hawks will buff everyone's assists, and more assists are always good, but if you don't want to double up or change pre-existing character specializations, you could also take:
Gunslinger
Medic
Heavy
Scout
Sharpshooter
I personally wouldn't recommend Medic or Scout. Medic is plain overkill early in the game when most combat encounters aren't that tricky (depending on your difficulty), and Scout is a class entirely about farming advantage, something you won't need to worry about much either in the game's initial missions.
Of the Gunslinger, Sharpshooter, and Heavy, I'd definitely recommend the former. Gunslinger is a strong early pick because of its ability to hit and finish off multiple enemies (getting you more advantage), plus its general buffs to ranged attacks. By comparison, Sharpshooter is more single-target focused, which can feel a bit limiting when you're not facing bosses or elite enemies, and the Heavy has more of a passive playstyle around taking hits and retaliating. This specialization works much better on an operator with the Taunt or Anticipation talent, allowing them to avoid or tank the damage better.
As you'll realise when you unlock operator recruitment, many of the best talents for recruitable operators are far more synergistic with specific classes than Hawk's Fearless Leader. Either way, don't be afraid to change specialisations often—it'll refund all of your Focus Points (apart from those in your character talent) so there's really no drawback to experimenting with party compositions.

title: How to respec your class and abilities in Star Wars Zero Company
text:
It's unclear whether you can respec Hawks when you first start out in Star Wars Zero Company , but the good news is you can, and it's an entirely free process. You can change class , but also refund every Focus Point you've spent in its dedicated tree to start levelling another. Here's how it's done.
How to respec in Star Wars Zero Company
You can respec at the Personnel console in your base Bit Reactor Focus Points will be refunded when you swap to a new specialization Bit Reactor You can change your class once you reach Cycle 3 , which is very early in the game. All you need to do is:
Interact with the Personnel console by the map table
Cycle right to the Focus Tree tab
Select Change Specialization in the bottom right
Pick whichever class you want
There's no cost to changing class and it will also refund all of your Focus Points, letting you respec entirely. The only thing this doesn't refund (if you're respec-ing a story character) is the Focus Points you've put into your talent at the top.
When you unlock recruitable operators a little later on, you'll also be able to change their talents in this same menu, letting you customise anyone you hire entirely. This means it's better to grab operators because you like the look of their character more than it is to recruit them based on their talent and specialization, which you can change at will.
While I do have some best class recommendations early on, it's well worth experimenting and playing around with different specializations. You can even change them on the initial story characters you work with like Trick and Kabb Uppercut, so team composition is always variable.

Picking the best talents in Star Wars Zero Company is something you'll start pondering when you unlock recruitable operators in the game. Each of these will have both a class and a talent, but the good news is that you can respec both in the change specialization menu once you've recruited them.
This means it's usually a better idea to recruit a character you like the look of, versus one with a talent you can tweak anyway. Some of these talents have a very clear and strong synergy with Zero Company's specializations, so I'll run through all available talents and talent levels below, plus give my top picks for each class.
All talents in Zero Company

Personally, I think the top-tier talents for any class are Life of Labor, Anticipation, and Grit . The former grants an all-round stat boost that's useful to pretty much every class, while the latter two give you ways to straight-up avoid damage. Anticipation, in particular, lets you dodge three attacks per turn at its highest level, which is somewhat cracked.
There are some obvious synergies between talents and classes, though. For example, the Heavy—a class all about taking hits—benefits from Taunt, Anticipation, or Grit, because it gives them a way to mitigate the damage more. Single-target focused Sharpshooters also benefit from Cold-Blooded, since you can combine the guaranteed crit with their guaranteed hit ability, or The Bigger They Are… to make them better at picking off elites.
And for more support-based classes like Medic or Scout, you can give them a way to avoid damage when out reviving someone with Anticipation, or make them support your wallet, too, by having them farm credits or intel with Thievery and Espionage respectively. I like giving Scout the Sabotage talent, which is incredibly situational, but feels very thematic, like they planted explosives before combat began.
